notes: A running account of where things stand by these headlines, revised after each edition rather than added to. Every version is kept.
Written by the model from the narratives, not from the headlines. It is a reading, not a record.
standing: On 8 November Trump called a return to war with Iran very unlikely, while Iraq's foreign minister said Washington had asked Baghdad to shut most of its border crossings with Iran. Al Jazeera described the largest naval gathering since the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and the Houthis struck at Riyadh and Aramco as Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa. A day earlier Italy let its diesel excise cut lapse, so diesel could rise by up to 5 cents a litre from 8 November, and Taiwan's CPC froze pump prices again after absorbing NT$34.07 billion. In Paraguay a court froze the assets of Santiago Peña, now reported as former president, and he was arrested over an estimated $809 million loss at the Ueno bank; Tesla raised the Cybertruck's price again and suspended orders for its entry version as Yangwang launched a flagship of about two million yuan in Abu Dhabi. Off Lompoul in northern Senegal at least 21 people died when a migrant pirogue capsized, and in Bangladesh a lottery shortlisted 300 applicants for 112 fee-free jobs in Malaysia.
moved: The Iran thread had a narrative again on 8 November, after two editions without one, and it turned: the war was reported paused. Trump called renewed war very unlikely, the US asked Iraq to shut crossings and gathered its largest fleet since 2003, and the fighting reported was between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The edition did not link it, so the Chronicle placed it by judgment.

Santiago Peña went from facing resumed impeachment proceedings on 6 November to having his assets frozen and being arrested on 8 November over the Ueno bank's estimated $809 million loss. The Chronicle placed the narrative carrying this in the failed-banks thread, and its join widened to declared wealth in the Philippines and Colombia and to trials of opponents in Armenia and Egypt.

The Chinese makers thread was carried on by its own edition for the first time since its revival. Tesla suspended orders for the Cybertruck's entry version, NIO says a plant completes a car a minute, Yangwang launched in Abu Dhabi and the Philippines said it will keep trading with China.

A thread began on routes to work abroad being rationed, with a Senegalese shipwreck, a Bangladeshi job lottery for Malaysia and a West Bengal deportation pledge. It was marked tentative, and four of its seven headlines came from one outlet.
silent: AI spending, parliaments refusing budgets and soldiers doing police work turned silent on 8 November after three editions without a narrative. For AI spending the quiet may be the sample's, since the 6 November report of Korean pension funds buying came without a narrative. For budgets and soldiers no headline in these editions has reported either way, and their expectations run to 30 November and 3 December.

Young people's protests stays silent. France's fourth weekend fell on 7 and 8 November, and neither edition reported a deployment; the expectation of 50,000 or more personnel is open only to 9 November.

Equipment orders, housing and platform feeds have gone two editions without a narrative, and one more turns them silent. Nothing in the 8 November edition suggests the world has moved on from them, so the quiet is more likely the sample's.

threads.label: Iran war, oil prices, talks and containment
threads.text: On 26 October the join was the Gulf running talks and strike preparations. From 27 October to 1 November it followed the Hormuz price shock to jet fuel, mortgages, wage rounds and a Turkish fuel tax. On 2 and 3 November it swung between talks and US strikes with the strait shut, and on 4 and 5 November it reached Congress and central bank rates. With no narrative on 6 and 7 November, tankers were reported hitting mines and the US striking again. On 8 November an unlinked narrative, placed here by the Chronicle, reported the war paused. Trump called a return to war very unlikely, the US asked Iraq to shut most crossings with Iran, the largest naval gathering since 2003 assembled, and the Houthis and Saudi Arabia struck each other's capitals and oil sites.
threads.direction: Since 7 November it has turned from who pays for the war's oil price to pressure on Iran by its land border and the sea, with the fighting reported on the Saudi-Houthi front.

threads.label: Governments ending fuel tax cuts mid-war
threads.text: Begun on 7 November and not linked by its edition to the Iran thread, though it keeps an expectation set there on 1 November. Italy will not extend its diesel excise cut, so diesel can rise by up to 5 cents a litre from 8 November. Portugal adjusts its fuel tax discount, Taiwan's state refiner CPC holds pump prices again after absorbing NT$34.07 billion, and a Japanese family lived in a tent inside its home after its electricity and gas were cut. The join is governments handing the war's fuel price back to drivers while the war goes on. Its case against says Italy and Portugal have adjusted these discounts since 2022, and the Japanese case names no war. No narrative carried it on 8 November, when the war was reported paused.

threads.label: War energy shock turned into equipment orders
threads.text: Begun on 6 November and not linked by its edition to the Iran thread, though it starts from the same war. Iran says two tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Siemens Energy says a Middle East power push is straining gas turbine supply, a Chinese solar cell line runs at full capacity, Adani Green turns to batteries for India's grid, and an agency finds the energy crisis speeding renewables in emerging economies. The join is that buyers who cannot lower the price of imported fuel are buying equipment to need less of it. Its case against says Siemens Energy's backlog and China's solar capacity predate the war, and some of these firms are sellers, not buyers. No narrative carried it on 7 or 8 November.

threads.label: Brazil's election and the United States
threads.text: On 26 October Brazil's vote was read as a script in Buenos Aires, Madrid and Nairobi. On 27 October Trump called the election rigged; by that evening, after Lula's run-off win, the United States was the common party in Flávio Bolsonaro's exit, Lula's warning of persecution, about 300 US soldiers in Colombia and Machado's return to Venezuela. Its events then ran under wider joins: Flávio's arrival in the United States and an amnesty plan for Jair Bolsonaro on 29 October, and Flávio's letter declaring himself president on 30 October. Brazil has since appeared inside other threads: as an oil producer, for its interest rate and rate cut, and on 6 November in the Banco Master case reaching Justice Alexandre de Moraes and in Brazilian savers funding US homes.
threads.direction: It moved from how Brazil's vote is read abroad to Washington's part in what follows, then was taken up under wider joins and fell silent.

threads.label: AI companies' listing, land and lawsuits
threads.text: On 26 October the join was an AI company listing the end of the world as a risk factor in its prospectus and the market buying the shares. Early on 27 October an edition followed data centres to county level, where land, grid and water requests were refused, and that morning Anthropic filed for a record US share listing as Elvis Presley's rights holders sued it over 200 songs. Data centres split into their own thread on 29 October. Late on 2 November Anthropic's quarterly loss went to the AI spending thread, and on 4 November Anthropic's IPO filing setting out risks appeared in the new thread on AI errors, not here.
threads.direction: It went from the prospectus to the ground and the courts, then fell silent as its subjects were carried under other AI threads.

threads.label: Young people's protests and their policing
threads.text: On 26 October the join was young people in public squares; on 27 October students struck or occupied buildings in France, Mexico, India and Italy. Revived on 31 October, when protests called for the same weekend met a ban in La Rochelle and negotiation in Lisbon, it was carried on 1 November with France deploying 70,000 security personnel for a third weekend and protesters detained in Poland. No headline reported a demand. No narrative has carried it since; on 5 November France's bill widening when police may fire went to the soldiers thread and French wage strikes to the budgets thread. Whether France deploys 50,000 or more for a fourth weekend, on 7 and 8 November, stays open until 9 November; neither the 7 nor the 8 November edition reported it.
threads.direction: It moved from youth as a political image to student strikes and then to policing reported as officers counted and routes diverted, then fell silent.

threads.label: Housing: state drives, protests and outside money
threads.text: On the morning of 27 October one narrative joined Egypt, Indonesia and Tamil Nadu expanding housing with Portugal investigating police at housing protests. After ten days without a narrative the Chronicle revived it on 6 November, by judgment, with an unlinked narrative marked tentative. Foreign buyers made 16% of Portuguese home purchases as prices hit records while 780,000 people left in five years, Brazilian firms raise up to R$400 million to build homes in the United States, and Australian essential workers are priced out of rents. The join is homes priced by money earned elsewhere; its case against says 84% of Portuguese purchases are by residents. No narrative carried it on 7 or 8 November; a migrant's return home from Portugal on 8 November went to the new thread on work abroad.
threads.direction: It moved from states building homes and police at protests to home prices set by buyers from outside, with Portugal in both editions.

threads.label: Public schemes passing costs to households
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. In six countries a public scheme meant to cover a cost was reported as falling short: Canadians paying for private surgery from savings and GoFundMe, German adult children billed for parents' care, Lucknow's subsidised generic pharmacies short of medicines, a Bangladeshi antivenom programme lacking funds, compensation claims from 50,000 Australians over Centrelink suspensions, and doubt over a Mexican voluntary pension scheme. The case against noted that several of these stories have run for years. No narrative has carried it since; the budgets thread begun on 2 November touched nearby ground but did not cite it.

threads.label: AI-made faces and files in checks
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. Nigeria's electoral commission is investigating suspected AI-generated photos in the voters' register, New Zealand job seekers report being ignored as AI-written applications flood employers, an Australian court passed the first sentence under deepfake laws without jail, and fashion models face AI copies of their image. The join is that a plausible picture or document now costs little to make while checking it still takes a person's time. No narrative has carried it since; the fake job interview behind the Binance theft went to the hacks thread on 3 November, and AI errors at Accenture to a new thread on 4 November.

threads.label: Broadcasts and films removed over offence
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. A Chinese platform dropped Racing-Real Madrid and La Liga broadcasts were suspended after a remark by Mbappé, an Indian court ordered a documentary on Adani and Modi taken down, a Korean drama faced calls to halt over a Gwangju episode, and Neil Young sued to stop Trump rallies using his songs. Three of the headlines were the same Mbappé story. No narrative has carried it since; on 6 November China's removal of 75,000 AI micro-drama titles went to the new thread on regulating platforms' feeds.

threads.label: AI spending: profit, sell-off, debt and hosts
threads.text: Begun on 29 October with Samsung and CHPT profits on data centre demand beside disputes in Norway, Finland and Russia. On 30 October it reached US growth credited to AI investment; on 31 October Alphabet had its biggest fall on record and Taiwan's state funds bought. On 1 November the falls were read as gains landing on few firms, and late on 2 November as a build needing lenders and hosts. On 5 November an unlinked narrative, placed here by the Chronicle, joined senior Democrats' call for a data-centre moratorium with a Nasdaq fall of more than 5% and foreign selling of NT$102.4 billion of Taiwanese shares. On 6 November, with no narrative, South Korean pension funds were reported buying 1.4 trillion won of shares as the KOSPI plunged. No narrative carried it on 6, 7 or 8 November, so it is silent.
threads.direction: It moved from profit and local objection through a sell-off and borrowing to the terms governments set, then fell silent with the falls reaching Seoul.

threads.label: Former leaders between courts and amnesty
threads.text: Begun on 29 October. South Korea's special counsel again sought, and by one report won, a death sentence for former president Yoon Suk Yeol over his martial law declaration, while in Brazil Alcolumbre planned an amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro and Flávio Bolsonaro reached the United States with Trump's consent. Spain's Zapatero, India's Azam Khan and Indonesia's anti-corruption law also appeared. No narrative has carried the court cases since. Najib Razak's fine on 6 November and Santiago Peña's arrest on 8 November went to the failed-banks thread, and Najib's conditional pardon on 7 November to the constitutions thread.

threads.label: Failed safety systems and operator blame
threads.text: Begun on 29 October and marked tentative by its own edition. A high-speed collision near Urda in Spain, which other headlines say killed 68 people, followed at least 15 warnings about faulty signalling; a JR train in Japan overran a station when its driver was drowsy and its automatic braking did not act; Bangladesh, Manila's airport and Mexico's networks had failures of grids, servers, cameras and internet. Only the Spanish and Japanese cases had a stated cause. No narrative has carried it since.

threads.label: Vote counts, rolls and election bodies contested
threads.text: Begun on 30 October with Flávio Bolsonaro declaring himself Brazil's president, Eisenkot accusing Netanyahu of delegitimising Israel's result and deletion forms in Delhi. On 2 November it took in Likud's doubt over the Knesset result, then moved before the vote: the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to halt California's count of 20,000 mail ballots and India's roll revision removed more than 90,000 names in Chamarajanagar. On 4 November a narrative placed here by the Chronicle moved it to election bodies in Mexico, Nigeria, South Africa and Israel. On 6 November, with no narrative, Trump was reported calling the US election rigged and demanding victory in Alaska's Senate race, keeping a 2 November expectation. No narrative has carried it since 4 November; a court request over a second state can come until 17 November.
threads.direction: It moved from disputing results to acting before polling and to who runs the commissions, and after the US vote a disputed result returned, by these headlines, without a narrative.

threads.label: Drones in war, numbers and arms production
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined drones cutting power, guarding a lake, carrying the wounded and being sold. Drones returned on 30 October, by the Chronicle's judgment, as a matter of numbers: a shortage of Ukrainian interceptors, a record raid shutting Moscow and St Petersburg airports, Finnish anti-drone training, Ukrainian loans to arms makers and Lithuanian conscription from 2032. No narrative has carried drones since; Ukrainian combat robots appeared in the AI thread on 1 November, and late on 2 November the seizure of two American drones near Qeshm appeared in the Iran thread.
threads.direction: It moved from the drone's many uses to the number of drones and the factories and conscripts states are raising to match them, then fell silent.

threads.label: Russia shunned by Europe, courted elsewhere
threads.text: Begun on 31 October. European ministers refused to stand beside Sergei Lavrov for the G20 photograph, while US and Russian foreign ministers discussed coordination at APEC, Washington weighed lifting sanctions on a Putin associate, Russia signed 53 documents at its Africa summit and Nigeria moved to replace a 1967 air agreement with Moscow. The case against says the Europeans still attended and the African deals renew old ties. No narrative has carried it since; its sanctions expectations are still open. On 3 November Kaliningrad's electronic warfare appeared in the Poland thread, and on 5 November Russia's record oil and gas revenue in the Iran thread.

threads.label: Courts and heads of state given the last word
threads.text: Begun on 1 November and marked tentative: Poland's president and Tusk's government fighting over the Constitutional Tribunal, Egypt's debate on amending the constitution and Madeira's revision; its case against said only Poland's was a crisis. After six editions without a narrative the Chronicle revived it on 7 November, by judgment, with an unlinked narrative also marked tentative. Lawyers say Vučić's pardons could go to Serbian courts and Strasbourg, Malaysia's Attorney General seeks an audience with the King over Najib Razak's conditional pardon, Taiwan's cabinet refuses to countersign an Elderly Welfare Act, and a Nigerian court voids Atiku's candidature. Its case against says the acts share form but not content. No narrative carried it on 8 November, when trials of opponents in Armenia and Egypt went to the failed-banks thread.
threads.direction: It moved from fights over who controls courts and constitutions to who has the last word on pardons and laws already passed.

threads.label: New ways of paying and their hidden costs
threads.text: Begun early on 2 November and marked tentative by its own edition. The Hindu explains that India's no-cost EMI is a loan presented as free; Yle reports Finnish shoppers annoyed by data collection but keeping their loyalty cards; Bangladesh launches a QR code for person-to-person payments while Jawa Pos defends Indonesians who still pay cash; and the FBI blames North Korea for the Binance theft. The join is that the visible fee has gone and the cost sits in a loan, a purchase record or an account the payer does not control. The Binance theft ran on in the hacks thread; no narrative has carried this join since, so it is silent.

threads.label: Budgets protecting pensions over working-age incomes
threads.text: Begun early on 2 November. Italy's budget promises no pension cuts up to 25,000 euros and faster severance for civil servants. Britain's John Healey promises the benefits bill will come down, Spanish economists say a self-employed worker on sick leave can have 180 euros for the month, and Russia reminds savers how to draw pension savings. The join is that income tied to age or a salaried contract is protected while income outside it is trimmed. Its case against says Italy's is the only budget and Healey is the defence secretary. No narrative has carried it since; on 5 November parliaments refusing budgets in France, Senegal and the Netherlands began a separate thread. Its expectations run to 30 November.

threads.label: Hacks through suppliers on freezers and wallets
threads.text: Begun late on 2 November with attacks on shop refrigeration hitting 17 Dutch businesses, which the EU called an attack on food supply, and North Korea denying the $6.3 billion Binance theft. On 3 November the edition carried it on and moved the join to how attackers get in: the Binance theft began with a fake job interview of an engineer, Singapore Airlines says 46,000 booking records were reached through Amadeus, Osaka City names may have leaked through an outside service, and Italian advice tells shops to check supplier contacts as the refrigeration attacks reach Belgium and Greece. Its case against says the supplier route for the shops rests on advice, not a finding. No narrative has carried it since 3 November, so it is silent.
threads.direction: It moved from what was hit, freezers and wallets, to the suppliers and staff through whom attackers got in, then fell silent.

threads.label: Unclaimed threats against Poland and its answers
threads.text: Begun on 3 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Emailed bomb threats forced a plane to land in Warsaw and diverted two Poland-bound planes from London; a second person was detained over the arson of a Starlink station; Onet reports Kaliningrad becoming a centre of electronic warfare, and GROM special forces were sent to the Russian border. The join is cheap, unclaimed acts drawing costly answers below the level at which NATO's treaty applies. On 5 November Corriere della Sera reported an emailed bomb alert on a Milan-Warsaw flight and Radio Zet an alarm at Chopin Airport, keeping the expectation of another such threat. No narrative has carried it since 3 November, so it is silent, likely by the sample. No headline yet names Russia.

threads.label: Chinese makers' gains and others' answers
threads.text: Begun on 3 November: SCG's chief executive told Fortune that China's cheap exports are a fact of life, Thailand raised taxes on imported electric cars and Tata Motors and Iveco formed a group. The Chronicle revived it on 7 November, by judgment: Musk said Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, BYD's Yangwang opened pre-orders for a 2.08 million yuan car and SAIC's Zhiji entered Brazil. On 8 November its own edition carried it on. Tesla raised the Cybertruck's price again and suspended orders for its entry version, NIO says a plant completes a car a minute, Yangwang launched its flagship in Abu Dhabi, a Xiaomi band sells for under €100 and the Philippines says it will keep trading with China. Its case against says three of six headlines are from Chinese portals and none reports a lost sale.
threads.direction: It moved from producers elsewhere merging or taxing to meet Chinese goods, to producers elsewhere retreating, and by 8 November to Chinese makers selling abroad at both the cheap and the luxury end.

threads.label: Foreign capitals reading the US midterm result
threads.text: Begun on 4 November, the day after the midterms. Iran's leaders called the result a rejection of Trump's war while Khamenei said Washington's Iran policy would not change; Egyptian commentators named Netanyahu among the losers; Pedro Sánchez said it would help Spain's socialists; Thai firms cheered; Canada's National Post asked whether Trump still wants a deal; Polish analysts expected no change in foreign policy. The join is that each capital reads the vote through its own dispute with Washington. Its case against says Trump himself linked the defeat to the war and several voices are commentators. No narrative has carried it since 4 November, so it is silent; on 8 November the Iran thread's case against read Trump's statement on war as possibly aimed at American voters after the midterms.

threads.label: Who answers for AI systems' errors
threads.text: Begun on 4 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Sina reports Accenture accused of publishing papers full of AI hallucinations after dismissing staff who would not use AI; Google has switched AI tools off by default for school pupils; an Italian trial of AI found it not chargeable but socially dangerous; Portuguese firms adopt AI faster than they train staff; Anthropic's IPO filing sets out the risks of its build; and NTT adds AI defences as attacks rise sevenfold. The join is that the consequences of errors land on whoever took a system up. Its case against says the Italian trial may be a staged debate and the Accenture item is an accusation. No narrative has carried it since 4 November, so it is silent.

threads.label: Parliaments refusing governments' budgets
threads.text: Begun on 5 November. French deputies unanimously rejected their government's budget ahead of nationwide wage strikes, Senegal's parliament asked for the 2027 budget bill to be withdrawn, Rob Jetten warned Dutch MPs that voting down his tax plan would cost billions, Japan's prime minister faces a time-limited committee session over a consumption tax cut, and a Democratic Congress must now fund the US government. The join is that governments no longer command the chambers that pass next year's taxes and spending. Its case against says autumn is budget season, first-reading rejections are common, and only the French and Senegalese cases are outright refusals. No narrative carried it on 6, 7 or 8 November, so it is silent; the Japanese cut bears on an expectation open to 28 November.

threads.label: Soldiers sent to keep civil order
threads.text: Begun on 5 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Indonesia's armed forces commander put troops in Jakarta and the army gave its own account of a deadly riot at a Maulid celebration in Aceh; Pakistan deployed the army and Rangers for Punjab by-elections; a Bangladeshi soldier was killed raiding traffickers at Teknaf; Lebanon's army ran raids and checkpoints with dozens arrested; and a French bill widening when police may fire was called an advance by police unions and a licence to kill by the left. The join is civil order handed to soldiers or to rules closer to theirs. Its case against says Pakistan's and Lebanon's arrangements are long-standing and the tasks differ. No narrative carried it on 6, 7 or 8 November, so it is silent.

threads.label: Regulators targeting platforms' recommendation systems
threads.text: Begun on 6 November. The European Commission accused TikTok of breaching EU rules through its content recommendation system; Google, Meta and TikTok are suing to block a California law restricting addictive social media features for children; China's broadcasting regulator opened a two-month campaign against vulgar and homogenised AI micro-dramas after removing 75,000 titles; and Democrats are preparing AI bills for Congress. The join is that the thing regulated is the system choosing what a user sees next, not a single post. Its case against says the three regulators want different things, China's campaign is content control of the old kind, and only the EU and California cases are clearly about ranking design. No narrative carried it on 7 or 8 November.

threads.label: Failed banks and money cases reaching office
threads.text: Begun on 6 November. Paraguay's Congress resumed impeachment of President Santiago Peña over the Ueno bank crisis, Daniel Vorcaro's phone recorded 316 interactions with Justice Alexandre de Moraes in the Banco Master case, Chile upheld a fine on Primus Capital's former chief executive, and UMNO's move to pay Najib Razak's RM50 million fine split Malaysia's coalition. On 8 November an unlinked narrative, placed here by the Chronicle because it follows the Peña case, reported a court freezing the assets of Peña, described as former president, and his arrest over an estimated $809 million Ueno loss. It added the Philippine vice-president answering wealth charges, scrutiny of a Petro official's income and opponents in Armenia and Egypt facing courts. Its case against says the Philippine case may itself be political and the Colombian item is a press inquiry.
threads.direction: It moved from failed banks reaching people in office to courts reaching office-holders through money in general, with Peña going from impeachment proceedings to arrest in two days.

threads.label: El Niño's first weeks arriving as rain
threads.text: Begun on 7 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Keiko Fujimori is reported visiting parts of Peru's Tumbes hit by rain; Pulzo reports that El Niño has not stopped thunderstorms and hail in Bogotá, and La Patria a landslide bringing trees down onto an avenue in Manizales; Brazil's Civil Defence has a 72-hour alert out and a downpour stopped Formula One qualifying at Interlagos. The join is that an El Niño expected as drought is arriving first as rain. Its case against says October and November are wet seasons in Colombia and south-eastern Brazil in any year, only one headline names El Niño, and only the Tumbes rain is out of season. No narrative carried it on 8 November.

threads.label: Routes to work abroad rationed and deadly
threads.text: Begun on 8 November and marked tentative by its own edition. Off Lompoul in northern Senegal a pirogue capsized and at least 21 people died. In Bangladesh a lottery shortlisted 300 applicants for 112 fee-free jobs in Malaysia, a testimony in Portugal's SAPO describes shared rooms and low pay ending a migrant's stay, and in West Bengal Suvendu Adhikari promised to deport every 'Bangladeshi infiltrator'. The join is that a person's attempt to work abroad is rationed by a draw, the sea, wages or expulsion. Its case against says the lottery may be meant to cut out recruitment agents, the shipwreck's destination is not given, the West Bengal pledge is about citizenship, and four of seven headlines come from bdnews24.

withdrawn.held: AI companies' share listings, the copyright suit against Anthropic and county refusals of data centre land, grid and water formed one thread.
withdrawn.undone: On 29 October data centres returned on their own, as profit for Samsung and CHPT and as planning and security disputes in Norway, Finland and Russia, with no listing or lawsuit in view. The land and power question is running apart from the companies' finance and courts, so the merge no longer holds.

withdrawn.held: The Iran war's price rise was moving outward from the pump to central bank rates and loan contracts, with the war named less often at each step.
withdrawn.undone: On 30 October the reports ran the other way: Washington pressing Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries and sending Tehran a peace proposal, Israel's pump price set to fall, Russia budgeting on $50 oil and US mortgage rates down for two weeks. The war was named directly again, and the costs were reported as easing more than spreading.

withdrawn.held: The data centre question was running apart from the AI companies' finance, as a matter of land, power and security.
withdrawn.undone: On 30 October the data centre thread itself turned to finance: US growth credited to AI investment, Amazon's spending and Alphabet's fall in market value, with no planning or security dispute in that edition. The split of threads stands, but the separation of data centres from company finance does not.

withdrawn.held: On 30 October the Iran war's costs had turned towards easing, with Washington pressing for a lower oil price before the midterms.
withdrawn.undone: On 31 October Brent rose 2.4% to $117.64, Italy's inflation reached 5.4% and the price rise was argued over in pay rounds and tax relief in several countries. The easing reading did not last a day, and the earlier withdrawal of the outward-spread reading now looks premature.

withdrawn.held: The AI share sell-off was moving towards losses partly taken on by Taiwanese public money, through its state funds and central bank.
withdrawn.undone: On 1 November no state buying was reported, and the same thread was read as AI money landing on a few chip and computing makers, with Micron staff payouts and Chinese results led by AI computing. The public-money reading rested on one edition and is not carried as the thread's direction.

withdrawn.held: The Iran war thread had turned to which governments carry the fuel price and which take more of it as revenue, with US-Iran talks stuck.
withdrawn.undone: On 2 November no fuel-tax argument appeared, Brent fell 2% to $111, Trump said talks were going well and the thread was about whether a strike or talks follow the US vote. The who-pays reading rested on Turkey's single tax rise and is not carried as the direction; its expectation of a second government raising a fuel tax is still open.

withdrawn.held: The AI spending thread had turned to how narrowly the gains land, on a few chip and computing makers and their staff.
withdrawn.undone: Late on 2 November the thread was about the build depending on borrowing, with Oracle and Meta raising about $20 billion each and Anthropic losing more than its revenue, and on governments and voters setting terms for data centres; no payouts were reported. The concentration reading rested on one edition and is not carried as the direction; its expectations stay open.

withdrawn.held: Late on 2 November the Iran thread was tilting towards talks, with prices falling on leaders' words while incidents at sea continued.
withdrawn.undone: On 3 November the edition reported the strait still shut as the US struck Iran, with a bombing at Qeshm on polling day; Qatar's mediation went on, but the force was American, not only incidents at sea. The talks tilt held for one edition, and the thread returned to who pays and who gains from the closure.

withdrawn.held: Central banks abroad, Brazil's among them with the world's highest real interest rate, were holding rates high against the Iran war's oil price.
withdrawn.undone: On 5 November Mexico's central bank cut to 6.25% and Brazil's continued to cut while the Bank of England raised to 4%. Holding high describes some importers, not rate-setters in general, and the Mexican and Brazilian headlines do not name the war.

withdrawn.held: The contested-count thread had moved on from disputing results after a vote to acting before polling and contesting the bodies that run elections.
withdrawn.undone: On 6 November Liputan6 reported Trump saying the US election was rigged and Svenska Yle reported him demanding victory in Alaska's close Senate race. Disputing a result after the vote is back in these headlines, so the thread has not left it behind.

withdrawn.held: On 7 November the US-Iran war was going on, with the US reported striking Iran again and the Revolutionary Guards saying their missile range limits were lifted.
withdrawn.undone: On 8 November the edition reported the war as paused, with Trump calling a return to it very unlikely and pressure moved to Iraq's border crossings and a naval build-up. The fighting reported that day was between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, not between the US and Iran.

withdrawn.held: Since 3 November the Iran thread had been following who pays for the war's oil price, a question that passed on 7 November to the thread on fuel tax cuts.
withdrawn.undone: On 8 November the thread's narrative named no price, rate or tax, and followed pressure on Iran by land and sea and the Saudi-Houthi exchange. The price question is not carried as this thread's direction; it sits in the fuel tax thread.

caseAgainst: This Chronicle rests on sixteen editions over about thirteen days, with none stamped 28 October, drawn from whichever publishers the collection reads and capped in how many headlines each may supply. On 8 November only one narrative continued an earlier one, so most joins between days are mine. I placed the unlinked Iran and Peña narratives in live threads by judgment, which reverses the choice I made on 7 November to keep the fuel tax narrative out of the Iran thread; the two practices are not consistent, and either could be argued. The Iran pause on 8 November sits a day after a reported US strike, and the difference may be in which headlines were caught, not in the war. The Peña narrative calls him former president two days after he was reported as president facing impeachment, and no headline here reports the step between. Three of six Chinese makers headlines came from Chinese portals and four of seven work-abroad headlines from bdnews24, so those threads may show the collection's shape more than the world's. I have led the standing with the war again, as every earlier version did.
line: On 8 November 2026 the US-Iran war is reported paused as Washington asks Iraq to shut its Iran crossings and the Houthis strike Riyadh and Aramco.
revision: The Iran thread took a narrative again, placed by judgment, and its direction was rewritten from oil prices to containment by border and sea, with two earlier readings withdrawn. Peña's arrest was placed in the failed-banks thread, which was relabelled, and a thread began on rationed routes to work abroad. AI spending, parliaments refusing budgets and soldiers doing police work turned silent, leaving ten threads live, and the standing was rewritten around the pause, Peña's arrest, Chinese makers and migrant work.
